item.mechanism: Poor ductility in two-phase RHEAs is caused by the continuous matrix being the ordered B2 phase, which is inherently brittle.
item.system: Al0.5NbTa0.8Ti1.5V0.2Zr in Condition (1) (cast, HIPed, homogenized at 1200°C/24h, slow cooled)
item.operating_conditions: Room temperature compression; microstructure consists of continuous ordered B2 matrix with discrete disordered BCC precipitates
item.supporting_observation: The alloy exhibited high yield strength (2035 MPa) but only 4.5% compression strain before fracture.
item.scope_limits: Does not apply to alloys where the BCC phase is continuous; the text notes this mechanism explains the brittleness of Al-containing RHEAs with superalloy-like microstructures.
item.alternatives_considered: Transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) or strain-induced precipitation, which the authors state cannot be applied to inherently brittle RHEAs that fracture without strain localization.
quotes: The poor ductility is attributed to the continuous matrix being the ordered B2 phase in these alloys.
The alloy has a room-temperature yield strength of 2035 MPa but only 4.5% compression strain before fracture in Condition (1).
The brittle nature of Condition (1) is due to the presence of continuous B2 channels.

item.mechanism: High ductility is achieved by inverting the microstructure to have a continuous disordered BCC matrix with discrete B2 precipitates, allowing dislocation mobility in the matrix.
item.system: Al0.5NbTa0.8Ti1.5V0.2Zr in Condition (3) (annealed at 600°C for 120 hrs after solutionizing)
item.operating_conditions: Room temperature compression; continuous disordered BCC matrix with discrete B2 precipitates (~50 nm)
item.supporting_observation: Condition (3) showed a true compressive fracture strain of 38% with a yield stress of 1345 MPa, significantly higher ductility than Condition (1).
item.scope_limits: The continuous BCC matrix provides ductility but results in lower yield strength compared to the continuous B2 matrix of Condition (1).
item.alternatives_considered: The authors note that while precipitation strengthening plays a role, the primary driver for the ductility increase is the change in the continuous phase from B2 to BCC.
quotes: The ductility of this alloy was substantially increased via microstructural engineering involving controlled annealing treatments, resulting in a phase inversion.
Consequently, the hard, ordered B2 compound that forms the continuous phase in Condition (1) is replaced by the more ductile, disordered, BCC phase in Condition (3).
While the higher B2 phase fraction is beneficial for strength, the continuous BCC matrix provides good compressive ductility.

item.mechanism: High strength in Condition (1) is attributed to strong element bonding in the continuous ordered B2 matrix, despite the resulting brittleness.
item.operating_conditions: Room temperature and 600°C compression; continuous ordered B2 matrix
item.supporting_observation: Condition (1) had the highest yield strength (2032 MPa at RT, 1774 MPa at 600°C) but low plasticity.
item.scope_limits: This mechanism is speculative; the authors state details of strengthening mechanisms are beyond the scope of the study.
item.alternatives_considered: Precipitation strengthening from B2 precipitates is considered less likely to be the primary cause of the extreme strength in Condition (1) compared to the continuous matrix effect.
quotes: It can be speculated that strong element bonding in the B2 matrix is responsible for high strength (and, unfortunately, brittleness) of Condition (1).
While the B2 matrix provides a very high strength to this condition, it suffers from rather poor ductility due to its ordered nature.
Condition (1) has the highest strength; Condition (2) has the highest compressive ductility; while Condition (3) provides a combination of high yield stress and good ductility.

item.mechanism: High ductility in Condition (2) is due to the material being largely a single-phase BCC alloy with small compositional fluctuations, allowing for significant strain hardening.
item.system: Al0.5NbTa0.8Ti1.5V0.2Zr in Condition (2) (solutionized at 1400°C, water quenched)
item.operating_conditions: Room temperature compression; single-phase BCC with weak B2 ordering
item.supporting_observation: The alloy did not show fracture even after 60% true strain, with a strain hardening rate of ~118 MPa.
item.scope_limits: This condition has lower yield strength (~1065 MPa) compared to the two-phase conditions (1 and 3).
item.alternatives_considered: The authors note that the weak B2 ordering in Condition (2) provides some strengthening but the primary factor for ductility is the disordered BCC matrix.
quotes: Condition (2) is largely a single-phase BCC alloy with a small degree compositional fluctuations, and thus has more ductility.
The alloy in Condition (2) showed continuous strengthening after yielding at a strain hardening rate dσ/dε ≈ 118 MPa.
Condition (2) was the weakest, as it is best characterized as a single-phase solid solution with no strengthening precipitates.

item.mechanism: Anomalous strengthening at 600°C (higher yield strength than at RT) in Condition (3) is speculated to be caused by cross-slip between competing slip systems in the B2 phase, creating sessile kinks.
item.operating_conditions: Compression at 600°C vs 25°C; continuous BCC matrix with discrete B2 precipitates
item.supporting_observation: Yield strength increased from 1345 MPa at 25°C to 1423 MPa at 600°C, an increase of about 6%.
item.scope_limits: The authors state this mechanism is highly speculative and the data needed to establish it are beyond the scope of the work.
item.alternatives_considered: Other mechanisms like cross-kinks or non-conservative dragging of jogs are also considered conceivable but speculative.
quotes: Such a mechanism is conceivable in the present alloy, since the B2 phase has many competing slip systems, including <001>{110} and <111>{112}.
The discussion offered here is highly speculative. The details of the deformation mechanisms at room temperature and at 600 °C for this RHEA require further investigation.

item.mechanism: The transition from a continuous B2 matrix to discrete B2 precipitates occurs via progressive increase in B2 channel width and eventual breaking up of channels during long-term annealing.
item.system: Al0.5NbTa0.8Ti1.5V0.2Zr transitioning from Condition (1) to Condition (3)
item.supporting_observation: Condition (1) has continuous B2 channels (~2 nm thick), while Condition (3) has discrete B2 precipitates (~50 nm) in a BCC matrix.
item.scope_limits: This mechanism describes the microstructural evolution path; it assumes the initial state was far-from equilibrium.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors note it is possible the alloy was undergoing phase separation at 1400°C, but the results suggest the initial microstructure formed during slow cooling.
quotes: This change in phase fractions is presumably accomplished via progressive increase in the width of the B2 channels (starting from Condition (1)), eventually leading to breaking up of these channels into discrete B2 precipitates.
Consequently, long-term isothermal anneal at 600 °C results in an increase in the B2 phase fraction accompanied by a reduction in the BCC phase fraction.

item.mechanism: High hardness in Condition (1) is due to the fine-scale decomposition into a two-phase B2 (hard) + BCC structure.
item.supporting_observation: Condition (1) had the highest hardness (562 ± 16 HV) compared to Condition (2) (405 ± 11 HV) and Condition (3) (475 ± 12 HV).
item.scope_limits: Hardness correlates with strength but does not directly measure ductility; the fine scale of the structure in Condition (1) contributes to high hardness but low ductility.
item.alternatives_considered: Condition (2) has lower hardness due to being a single-phase weakly ordered BCC structure.
quotes: The highest hardness was found in Condition (1) due to its fine-scale B2 (hard) + BCC decomposed microstructure, as compared to the single-phase weakly ordered BCC microstructure in Condition (2).

Intermediate hardness was observed in Condition (3) due to the presence of discrete B2 precipitates within the continuous BCC matrix, since the scale of the two-phase BCC + B2 microstructure in Condition (3) is substantially coarser than Condition (1).
Microstructure showed the same influence on strength as for hardness.

item.mechanism: Transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) approaches are not applicable to inherently brittle RHEAs that fracture without strain localization.
item.system: General class of Al-containing RHEAs with continuous B2 matrix (like Condition 1)
item.operating_conditions: Tensile or compressive loading where fracture occurs without necking
item.supporting_observation: The authors state that TRIP approaches work for intrinsically ductile RHEAs but fail for those that fracture without macroscopic strain.
item.scope_limits: This limitation applies specifically to the class of Al-containing RHEAs with superalloy-like microstructures described in the paper.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors propose microstructural engineering (phase inversion) as the alternative approach for these brittle alloys.
quotes: Unfortunately, this method is only applicable to intrinsically ductile RHEAs that show low tensile ductility due to rapid strain localization and necking.
It cannot be applied to inherently brittle RHEAs that fracture without strain localization/necking and, often, without any macroscopic strain.
Unfortunately, the approaches for improving ductility discussed above cannot be applied to this class of Al-containing RHEAs.
